title: Lesson 5: Suffering and Trials
description: When life gets hard, you are often holding one jagged piece of a picture you cannot see. Through Joseph's story, this lesson shows a God who sees the whole of it, stays near in the valley, and can be trusted when you do not know why.

blocks.text: In the last lesson, you began to notice the gifts Jesus has placed in you. Those gifts get used in a broken world, and sooner or later a hard season comes. This lesson is about suffering: what God is doing in it, who is with you in it, and how to trust Him when you cannot see the whole picture.

blocks.alt: Dark prison bars on the left opening to Joseph in the sunlit Egyptian granary welcoming his bowed brothers beside sacks of grain

blocks.title: The Pit, the Prison, and the Palace
blocks.text:
Joseph was seventeen, his father's favorite son, and his older brothers hated him for it. They tore off the special robe his father had given him and threw him into an empty pit. He begged them, and they would not listen (Genesis 42:21). Then they sold him to traders headed for Egypt and let their father believe he was dead.

In Egypt, Joseph became a slave in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. He served faithfully, but Potiphar's wife lied about him, and Joseph was thrown into prison for something he did not do. Even there, the Bible says, "the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love" (Genesis 39:21). He explained a dream for Pharaoh's cupbearer and asked only to be remembered. The cupbearer forgot him for two whole years.

Then Pharaoh had dreams no one could explain, and the cupbearer finally remembered. Joseph went from the prison to the palace in a single day and was put in charge of storing grain before seven years of famine. When the famine came, his brothers traveled to Egypt for food and bowed before the brother they had sold, without knowing who he was.

More than twenty years after the pit, Joseph wept and told them who he was. Years later, when his brothers feared he would finally pay them back, Joseph said, "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today" (Genesis 50:20).

Joseph did not get to skip to the last chapter. He spent about thirteen years as a slave and a prisoner, and the Bible does not pretend those years were easy. But the LORD was with him in every one of those places, working in ways Joseph could not yet see.
5.1 - What is the hardest season you are walking through right now, or have walked through in the last few years?
Suffering Is Real
If God is good and powerful, then why does life hurt so much? That question is not a sign of weak faith, and God is not offended when you ask it.

Suffering comes in more than one kind. Some pain comes from living in a broken world, like sickness, loss, and grief. Some comes from sin, whether that is the fallout of your own choices or a wound someone else gave you. And some comes because you belong to Jesus, who said, "If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you" (John 15:20). These can overlap, and you will not always know which one you are in.

So be careful with the idea that suffering is always punishment. When the disciples saw a man who was born blind, they asked whose sin had caused it. Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents" (John 9:3). People live very different lives, but each person feels their own pain. Your pain is real, and it does not mean God has stopped loving you.
God Meant It for Good

Look closely at what Joseph said to his brothers. He did not pretend the evil was not evil. You meant evil against me. His brothers chose their cruelty, and they were responsible for it. But Joseph also said, God meant it for good. God was not the author of their sin, and He was not surprised by it. He rules over all things, and He wove even their evil into His plan to keep many people alive, including the brothers who sold him.

Picture a mosaic, a large image made from hundreds of small pieces of colored glass. Hold one piece close to your eye and it may look cracked, sharp, and dark, with nothing beautiful about it. Step back, and that same piece turns out to be part of a sunrise. The piece did not change, but now you can see where it belongs.

In a hard season, you are usually holding one piece. Joseph in the prison could not see the palace, the famine, or the family he would save. Job never got to read the book of Job. He only got to live it. God does not always show you the whole picture, but He is the Artist, and He sees all of it. You do not have to see the whole mosaic to trust the Artist.

The clearest proof is the cross. On that Friday, the death of Jesus looked like the darkest and most jagged piece of all. Wicked men meant it for evil, but God meant it to save the world, and three days later the tomb was empty. Some of your own picture you may not see until eternity, when "the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18).

A word of care. Trusting the Artist is not the same as calling evil good. Cancer is not good, and betrayal is not good. If someone has abused you, Joseph's words do not mean that what they did was acceptable or that you must stay in danger. If you are not safe, tell a pastor or a trusted friend and get help today.
5.2 - When you read "God meant it for good," what is your first honest response: hope, resistance, or something else?
The Valley Refines You
The mountaintops encourage you, but the valley refines you. James, the brother of Jesus, wrote to believers who were walking through one.

Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.

James does not say to feel happy about suffering. He says to count it joy, a choice that rests on what you know and not on what you feel. This is not a smile you force, and it can sit right beside tears. What you know is that God can use a hard season the way a refiner uses fire, to grow steadier faith, a humble heart, and a tenderness toward other hurting people. You do not have to prove any growth today. But God does not waste the valley.
5.3 - Looking back on a hard season, what did God grow in you that might not have grown any other way?
You Are Not Alone in It

Jesus did not promise His followers a life without trouble. He said, "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33). What He promised was Himself. Peace is not the absence of conflict, and it is not the absence of suffering. Peace is the presence of God. You can have Him near while the hard thing is still hard, so bring Him your honest pain and your raw questions. The Psalms are full of both.

God also comes near through His family. The Bible says to "weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15), and it does not add a speech. Sometimes the silent person sitting next to you helps more than a book on suffering. So let someone in. Tell one trusted person what you are carrying, as much or as little as you choose. Reaching out to a pastor, a doctor, or a counselor is a way of receiving God's care too.

When a friend is the one hurting, you can be that person for them. Listen without needing the details. Bring a meal, give a ride, or just stay. You do not have to explain what God is doing. The comfort God has given you is often the best thing you have to give (2 Corinthians 1:4).
5.4 - Who in your life is walking through a hard season, and how could you walk alongside them this week?
This Week's Practice

This week, pray Psalm 13, 42, or 88 out loud. Each one is a lament, an honest prayer of pain. Even Psalm 88, which ends in the dark, is still a prayer. You do not have to fix the feeling. You only have to bring it to the right Person.

Then write down one hard thing you are carrying. Beneath it, write: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18). If you can, add: I trust the Artist. You may not feel it yet, and that is all right.
Lesson 5 Review

Suffering is real, and the Bible does not hide from it. In a hard season you are often holding one jagged piece, but God sees the whole mosaic, as He did for Joseph. The cross and the empty tomb show what He can make from the darkest piece of all. He is near in the valley, and He sends His family to sit beside you. You do not have to see the whole picture to trust the Artist.
In the next lesson, you will meet two men who sang in a prison at midnight, and see why worship is the natural response to who God is.
